Ron: Susan, have you decided what you want to study yet?
Susan: I have really started to enjoy my anthropology course. I've been fascinated by other cultures and learning about customs and ways of life that are different from ours for years. If I major in anthropology, I'll get to travel to other parts of the world. If I do well, I could even get a job abroad when I finish. What about you? Did you decide to stick with sciences?

Ron: For now I've opted for psychology. Learning how the brain works caught my interest. But if I continue with it, I won't be able to pursue my real interest.
Susan: Which is?
Ron: Robotics. If I want to study that, I'll have to transfer to engineering.
Susan: Really? I didn't know you could study robotics here!

Ron: You can! It's fascinating! Did you know that robots have already started to perform surgical operations? Of course they've worked in factories and automobile plants for a while now. I also read an article about Japanese robots designed to help physically disabled people.
Susan: Sounds great. However, if we don't watch out, they'll replace people! I do want to get a job when I graduate.
Ron: Don't worry, Susan. As far as I know, there aren't any robot anthropologists yet!

The First Conditional
You can use the first conditional to talk about actions and situations in the future.
There are two parts to the sentence. One part is the condition. The other part is the result.

Form:
If + subject + Simple Present tense + subject + will/won't
You use a comma after the condition in this form.
You can flip the two parts of the sentence so that the result comes first. You don't use a comma if you start with the result clause.  It can be in interrogative form.

Form:
Will/Won't + subject + if + subject + Simple Present tense ?

Present Perfect Tense vs. Past Simple

You use the Present Perfect tense to talk about a finished action or event that is connected to the present in some way.

You use the Simple Past tense to talk about a finished action or event not necessarily connected to the present.

You can use the Present Perfect tense to talk about experiences. When you use the Present Perfect tense, you think about the past and present together. There is some connection between what happened in the past and now.
To help you decide whether you should use the Present Perfect tense or the Past Simple tense, ask yourself the question ‘When?'
If you can answer the question ‘When?', because the past time is stated or inferred or understood, use the Past Simple. There is no connection to the present.
If the you cannot answer the question ‘When?', because the time is not stated or not important, then choose the Present Perfect tense. There is instead a connection to the present.
